analysis.investment_thesis: Cigniti is a financially disciplined, near-debt-free IT testing specialist with impressive ROCE of 34% and steadily expanding revenues — but software QA is a commoditizable niche increasingly threatened by AI-automated testing, and its new subsidiary status under Coforge creates structural minority shareholder risk that Munger would find deeply uncomfortable.
key_strengths: Exceptional capital efficiency: ROCE 34.1%, ROE 26%, Debt/Equity near zero (borrowings collapsed from ₹121 Cr in 2020 to ₹20 Cr in 2025)
Revenue compounding at 14.5% CAGR over 9 years with OCF positive all 5 years and FCF of ₹147 Cr in FY25
Cheap valuation at 11.7x P/E and 9x EV/EBITDA for a profitable, growing IT services business
key_risks: AI disruption is existential: generative AI tools that write and run tests autonomously directly attack Cigniti's core business model
Subsidiary of Coforge since Dec 2024 — minority shareholders face classic risks: related-party pricing, potential delisting squeeze-out at unfavorable terms
Weak moat — IT testing has no pricing power or structural lock-in; TCS, Infosys, Wipro all have competing QA practices at scale
red_flags: 2017 net loss of -₹395 Cr (massive write-down) reveals historical financial fragility and raises questions about past management discipline
FCF/Net Income of 73.5% (₹147 Cr / ₹200 Cr) falls below my 80% quality threshold — earnings slightly outpacing cash reality
Operating income was deeply erratic for years (₹-22 Cr in 2017, ₹52 Cr in 2018) — consistency of a quality business this is not
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Invert first: what kills this business? Generative AI writing, running, and maintaining test suites is not a distant threat — it's happening now. A pure-play software testing firm is precisely the profile most vulnerable to AI automation hollowing out billable hours. Munger's mental model from physics applies: when the environment changes, organisms without an adaptive moat go extinct. Cigniti's financials look good today precisely because the business hasn't yet been disrupted — but quality testing work increasingly flows toward platforms, not service firms. The ROCE of 34% and debt-free balance sheet are genuinely excellent, but these metrics reflect a business in its prime before structural headwinds accelerate.

The Coforge subsidiary dynamic adds a governance layer Munger would find troubling. Minority shareholders in a listed subsidiary are perpetually at the mercy of the parent's capital allocation decisions, transfer pricing, and — most critically — potential delisting at the parent's chosen timing and price. The promoter stake of 54% (now Coforge) means minority interests are structurally subordinated. At P/E 11.7x and EV/EBITDA 9x, the market appears to already price in some of this uncertainty, but "cheap" is not a margin of safety when the business model faces secular disruption. This is a fair business at a fair price — not the great business at a fair price Munger demands.
